What is the FlexIndex?

The FlexIndex is a comprehensive composite index created specifically to help operators, investors, and stakeholders navigate the flexible workspace industry with confidence and clarity.

By providing quarterly, data-driven insights, it helps inform strategic decisions, optimize operational performance, and benchmark against global and regional industry standards.

The report delivers detailed regional breakdowns, allowing you to assess how your business stacks up against competitors and industry peers. At the heart of the FlexIndex are six critical KPIs selected for their relevance and actionable insights:

  1. Desk Occupancy – Reflects the utilization of flexible desks, a core indicator of workspace demand.
  2. Revenue Occupancy – Measures how effectively available space is monetized.
  3. Private Office Occupancy – Tracks trends in demand for private, secure office solutions.
  4. Revenue per Occupied Desk (RevPOD) – Evaluates revenue generation efficiency per desk.
  5. Revenue per Available Desk (RevPAD) – Captures the overall revenue efficiency across total workspace inventory.
  6. Price per Hour of Booking – Indicates trends in pricing and booking rates.

Key Global Insights from Q1 2025

The latest FlexIndex data highlights the flex workspace industry’s resilience and growth momentum. Operators around the world are successfully adapting their strategies to shifting market dynamics and consumer preferences.

  • Private Office Occupancy exhibits significant regional variations. Some regions are experiencing robust growth, reflecting increased demand for stable, private office solutions. In contrast, the slight decline in other regions highlights evolving work patterns, necessitating region-specific strategies.

Diving Deeper: Understanding KPI Trends

Revenue per Occupied Desk (RevPOD) continues to demonstrate the effectiveness of smarter, demand-based pricing strategies. Operators who proactively adapt their offerings and pricing models are building stronger foundations for sustained profitability.

Revenue per Available Desk (RevPAD) has shown incremental improvements, although regional disparities suggest opportunities for further optimization in aligning supply with demand.

By closely analyzing these metrics, you can swiftly identify trends, respond to emerging opportunities, and adjust strategies for maximum impact.

Methodology You Can Trust

To ensure the highest standards of accuracy and reliability, the FlexIndex employs a rigorous data collection and analysis process:

  • Extensive Data Collection: Aggregated monthly from over 2,000 active coworking locations worldwide.
  • Data Filtering and Quality Assurance: Excludes canceled and free bookings, unrealistic booking durations, and bookings with zero or negative pricing.
  • Membership Revenue: Excludes service-type membership plans for consistency.
  • Organizational and Outlier Exclusions: Systematically removes predefined organizations and data points that fall outside realistic occupancy and revenue ranges.
  • Currency Standardization: Converts all financial metrics into USD for consistent, global comparison.

Fluctuations and Trends: Keeping Perspective

It’s important to note that quarter-to-quarter fluctuations are natural and often seasonal. While these short-term deviations can seem alarming, they typically represent temporary shifts rather than enduring trends.

Comparing your data year-over-year, rather than quarter-to-quarter, offers a more accurate picture of long-term performance and growth trajectories.

Name: 5 Tips To Build A Successful Coworking Community
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Successful coworking communities have always been a noticeable trait that attracts people to shared spaces. The opportunity to be part of something bigger. Of something truly amazing. A reason to put on pants.
Post body:
Successful coworking communities have always been a noticeable trait that attracts people to shared spaces. The opportunity to be part of something bigger. Of something truly amazing. A reason to put on pants.

A coworking community is the network of members inside a shared workspace who connect, collaborate, and support each other’s work, turning a room full of desks into a place people actually want to be.

Research published by Harvard Business Review states that the number one reason people move from a traditional office environment to shared spaces is to have access to a community that helps them grow and create connections.

In addition, the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor shows that entrepreneurs form a kind of community, united by their networking and shared aspirations. It’s easier to grow a business when you’re surrounded by people who have similar values and interests. A place where networking and collaboration opportunities are countless.

Community remains the clearest differentiator for coworking spaces, and it matters more than ever as the sector matures. Corporate demand is now a primary growth driver, with 55% of corporations using flexible workspace. So if you’re looking to scale, how do you go about building a community that holds? After working with hundreds of coworking spaces around the world, we’ve noticed some interesting commonalities in the approach to successfully scaling a community.

Here’s what we’ve observed so far.

#1 Know your mission and define your audience

Good communities are a well-balanced mixture of shared mindset (vision, values, interests, etc) and diverse skills. When a group of people has a similar focus coupled with diverse expertise, they can complement each other by sharing good practices and exchanging know-how in a way that’s applicable.

For example, one of our clients, Alley, focuses on growing the connectivity points between individuals and entrepreneurs and adding to the value they bring to the community. They position themselves as a “connected platform for entrepreneurs”, which directly speaks to what type of members they’ll welcome in the space. The result? When you walk into any of their spaces the entrepreneurial spirit is evident.

So where do you start? Be clear on what your vision and mission are and communicate them properly. Define your target audience and make sure you understand what they care about and what you bring to the table. If this sounds a bit too broad, start by asking yourself questions like:

  • “What type of companies or individuals do I want to attract?”
  • “Why should they care about me and being part of this community?” (If your answer is because of the good location, interior design, price, etc, and doesn’t explain how you’ll help them succeed, then something is missing.)
  • “What values should they share that will increase the chance of success of each member in the space?”

#2 Think about your member journey

Consider your member journey from start to finish; from coming for a tour to becoming a member. What can you do in each stage to make sure that when the time comes, you’ll be able to point them in the right direction (or better yet, introduce them to the right person)?

The breakdown of the member journey will be different for each coworking space, but here’s an example that illustrates our point:

Pre-sales stage

You can start simply by asking potential members questions like “Why do you want to join our community?”. Alternatively, if there is high demand for your space and you have the luxury to “source” the right candidates, you can go as detailed as sending qualification questionnaires or doing “entry interviews” with potential members.

Ask them about their goals, interests, motivations to join your space, or anything else that will help you come up with ideas on how to help them down the line.

Onboarding stage

Usually, onboarding checklists come into play here. But it also might make sense to set aside some time with them to discuss all the info you gathered during the sales process. Just a casual conversation that helps you dig a bit deeper into the info they provided, so you can come up with ideas about people or events they might be interested in.

Active member stage

It’s a good practice to set up follow-up tasks and check on how your recommendations and introductions turned out, but you’ll probably need to do more than that to keep your members engaged.

It’s hard to recommend a specific set (or type) of activities that are the formula to success, as each community is unique. What we’ve noticed is that every coworking space that developed a vibrant and engaged community says that events are key.

Invest consistent effort in engaging people. In coworking, the real magic happens offline, but make sure you take advantage of online tools to engage your community as they encourage interactions and help keep your members informed.

Eventually, if you’ve made sure your community consists of members with similar interests and you’ve done your best to keep them engaged, things should start developing on their own. Just give the initial push and then make sure to provide a good environment for things to happen.

The final bit that comes into play: someone left your coworking space, but does this mean that your community is 1 person (or team) short?

Best case scenario, it shouldn’t. So we want to give special emphasis to the final stage of the member’s journey:

#3 Extend your community to people outside of your space

A community is not defined by time and space limitations but by the value and the meaning of the interactions between people. Retaining former members in your community, or establishing connections with members’ friends who share similar values and interests can be useful as they might have the expertise to help your current members (and vice versa).

Think about the people you met at college or university. Although you’re not going to classes anymore, you probably still keep in touch with the ones you’ve had meaningful interactions with. It’s not a coincidence that the best universities like Stanford, Oxford, and Cambridge have top-notch alumni associations, which are the communities that gave birth to many of the most successful companies (take Instagram for example, whose co-founders met through the Stanford alumni network).

However, once your community grows above a certain point, it becomes impossible to rely only on your memory to make such meaningful introductions. So how do you keep up?

Here’s a resource on community building worth reading.

Maintain some kind of database

Whether you’re using a coworking CRM, a spreadsheet or some kind of dedicated tool, you’ll need a way to keep track of all essential information and make it easily accessible. You can also come up with some sort of tagging mechanism to source the information you need.

Set up an online community

Think about how you can use technology to increase member visibility and let people connect with each other directly. An online community that grows on its own and can be nurtured with less effort. You have members who love dogs? Invite them and make your space dog-friendly for the occasion.

#4 Foster inclusivity and diversity

Inclusivity and diversity are now core traits of successful coworking communities. A diverse community brings together different perspectives, ideas, and skills, which lead to better collaborations. The demographic reflects this shift: the average coworking member is now 38 years old, up from 35 in 2020, and women make up close to half of members. To build a community that works for that range of people:

  • Host diverse events: organize events that cater to different interests, cultures, and professional backgrounds.
  • Promote equal opportunities: make sure all members have access to the same resources, opportunities, and platforms to share their ideas and projects.
  • Create a welcoming environment: make sure your space is accessible and welcoming to people of all backgrounds, including those with disabilities.

#5 Facilitate networking and collaboration

One of the primary reasons professionals choose coworking spaces is the chance to network and collaborate with like-minded people. To make that easier:

  • Community events: regularly host networking events, skill-sharing sessions, and team-building activities.
  • Collaboration tools: give members digital tools where they can connect, share ideas, and work together on projects.
  • Community manager: employ a dedicated community manager who actively introduces members to each other and builds connections.

How software supports your coworking community

Once your community grows past a couple dozen members, memory and spreadsheets stop scaling. This is where a coworking platform earns its keep. OfficeRnD Flex is coworking space software that helps operators manage daily operations and keep members connected in a single system.

OfficeRnD Flex makes it easy to build genuine community in a coworking space, not just manage it. Members can connect with each other, stay in the loop on events, and engage with their space right from a branded mobile app – while operators get the tools to keep that engagement running smoothly behind the scenes. It’s less about software for software’s sake, and more about giving people real reasons to show up and stick around.

Bonus tip

Being focused on hospitality is essential for the success of coworking spaces. But be careful how far you stretch your hospitality service, as too much of it can ‘steal’ the feeling of commitment to the community. Be caring, but let people take the initiative too.

Here’s a simple example: if a member comes to you with an idea for an event that might interest other people in the space, let them actively take part in organizing it.

Conclusion

Whether it lets companies meet a new client without leaving the office, helps young startups grow, or simply gives people a chance to share knowledge, a strong community adds both human and business value.

Community is the core of a coworking space. It’s what attracts people. It’s often difficult to explain, yet it’s why we’re all in love with coworking.

Name: Introducing Bulk Bookings: The First Of Its Kind Resource Booking Powerhouse
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Bulk Bookings is a feature in OfficeRnD Workplace that lets admins and team leads reserve multiple desks and spaces for a group of people in one action, straight from the office map.
Post body:
Bulk Bookings is a feature in OfficeRnD Workplace that lets admins and team leads reserve multiple desks and spaces for a group of people in one action, straight from the office map.

If you manage seating for a team, you know the old way: open a resource, pick a desk, assign a person, repeat. Bulk Bookings replaces that with a single click-and-drag on the floor plan. Here’s what it does and how to use it.

What is Bulk Bookings?

Bulk Bookings is part of OfficeRnD Workplace. It reserves several bookable resources, such as desks and spaces, at the same time for a set of employees or an entire team.

Say your sales team is coming in on Tuesday and you want them sitting together. Instead of booking each desk one at a time, you select a block of desks on the map, add the team, and confirm. Everyone gets a desk near their colleagues, and each person receives an email invite.

You can book desks for a group in a few clicks, which saves the repetitive admin work of assigning seats individually and cuts the chance of double bookings.

Why we built Bulk Bookings

This came from direct requests by the people who run day-to-day resource management: admins, office managers, and team leads booking on behalf of colleagues.

Coordinating dozens of separate bookings by hand took time and led to mistakes. Bulk Bookings handles the whole group in one pass, so a team day out or an all-hands seating plan takes minutes instead of an afternoon.

What are the key benefits?

  1. Time saved: Book multiple desks and spaces in one action. No repetitive entries or switching between booking screens.
  2. Fewer errors: Every reservation is tied to a specific user and recorded together, which reduces double bookings and scheduling conflicts. If someone is booked as out of office or already has a reservation that day, you’re warned before you confirm.
  3. Simpler group management: Handle team days, workshops, and department seating without booking person by person.
  4. Teams sit together: Place colleagues next to each other for the days when being in the same room matters.

How does Bulk Bookings work?

A Workplace admin enables the feature first, under Settings > Organization > Booking Permissions by turning on Allow Bulk Bookings. By default you can book 15 resources at once. You can set that limit anywhere from 2 to a maximum of 25.

Once it’s on, here’s the flow:

  1. In the Web Portal, open the Office Map.
  2. Click the Bulk Booking button. This opens the full-page office map.
  3. Click or drag to select the desks and/or spaces you want to reserve, then click “Bulk Book.”
  4. Use the search field to add individual employees or a whole team (for example, the Sales team). If members are out of office or already have a reservation that day, you’ll be notified before you finalize. You can also add a message or description for the group.
  5. Choose the rest of your booking options and click “Book.” The bookings are created and email invitations go out to each attendee.

A few things worth knowing. Meeting rooms and assigned resources can’t be booked in bulk; all other bookable resources, including desks and spaces, can. Each attendee is matched to one of the selected resources. If you pick more resources than people, the extras are left free. And if any booking fails, the system tells you how many went through, how many didn’t, why, and which users couldn’t be booked.

Who benefits from Bulk Bookings?

  • Administrators and facility managers: Manage seating at scale and reduce booking errors.
  • Team leaders: Coordinate team days and make sure everyone has a desk when they arrive.
  • Office managers and executive assistants: Arrange seating for groups and events without booking each person separately.
Important: Bulk Bookings is available for Pro and Enterprise customers. Click here to check out our plans.

Frequently asked questions

How many desks can I book at once with Bulk Bookings?

The default is 15 resources per bulk booking. A Workplace admin can change that limit to anywhere between 2 and 25 in Settings > Organization > Booking Permissions.

Can I book meeting rooms in bulk?

No. Meeting rooms and assigned resources aren’t eligible for Bulk Bookings. Desks and other bookable spaces are.

Does Bulk Bookings support recurring bookings?

No. Bulk Bookings applies to a specific date and doesn’t support recurrences. For repeating reservations, use the separate recurring bookings feature in OfficeRnD Workplace.

Which plans include Bulk Bookings?

Bulk Bookings is available on the Pro and Enterprise plans.

What happens if someone in the group is already booked or out of office?

You’re notified before you confirm. If a booking still fails, the system reports how many went through, how many didn’t, the reason, and the names of anyone who couldn’t be booked.

Try Bulk Bookings

Open your OfficeRnD Workplace portal to get started. If the button isn’t there yet, ask your Workplace admin to enable it under Booking Permissions.

Not an OfficeRnD Workplace customer? Start a 14-day free trial and see the feature in action.

Name: How To Chart A Digital Transformation Roadmap [For 2023]
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Digital transformation represents a profound change for your organization. It refers to the adoption of new digital tools and technologies to revolutionize how your company does business.
Post body:
Digital transformation represents a profound change for your organization. It refers to the adoption of new digital tools and technologies to revolutionize how your company does business.

But even organizations with the most forward-looking strategies will struggle if they don’t know how to enact them.

That’s why you need a digital transformation roadmap.

A digital transformation roadmap is the pathway from your goals to your results. It lays out the actions and tactics that will help create a successful business transformation.

This article will explain why these roadmaps matter and how to create one.

Then, we’ll go into how digital transformation roadmaps intersect with hybrid operations specifically and give you some real-world examples of these roadmaps put to use.

Quick Summary

  • A successful digital transformation roadmap helps a company’s transformation goals become a digital reality.
  • Hybrid work environments intensify the need for new technologies and digital processes to facilitate idea-sharing and a more collaborative environment.
  • Successful digital transformation, especially in hybrid models, relies heavily on leadership engagement, feedback-gathering tools, appropriate technology, and high-impact digital initiatives.

What Is a Digital Transformation Roadmap?

A digital transformation roadmap is a high-level plan that outlines the steps needed to connect your strategic vision to your digital transformation goals. A roadmap makes your digital transformation strategy clear, focused, and measurable.

Digital transformation involves incorporating new technologies into all aspects of a business, leading to dramatic shifts in:

  • Operations and strategy
  • Customer engagement
  • Internal processes

This profound change can be seen all around us. In fact, McKinsey & Company predicts the upcoming decade will see more technological advancements than the previous 100 years combined.

However, for your transformation strategies to work, you need direction. That’s where a digital transformation roadmap comes into play.

There’s no simple formula or one-size-fits-all solution.

To quote a 2022 research report in the Global Strategy Journal: “…digital transformation will likely look different and be different for different executives, even for those whose firms compete in the same industry or country.”

3 Key Aspects of a Digital Transformation Roadmap

Here are three key aspects of digital transformation that can help you map out your plan and its execution:

The Customer Experience

By using the right technology, businesses can enrich customer interactions and offer previously impossible levels of engagement. That promises long-term dividends.

PwC found in their 2023 Global Consumer Insights Pulse Survey that a majority of consumers have purchased products directly from a brand’s website. They expect that number will only grow.

This speaks to a broader trend: Consumers aren’t just interested in the cheapest price — they want to connect with and support their favorite companies.

Data and Analytics

In our increasingly digital world, data isn’t hard to come by. The real challenge is interpreting that data and successfully applying the insights you gain from it.

These analytics aren’t just about understanding the past but also helping to predict the future. Additionally, they drive a more personal experience for customers, increasing their satisfaction and loyalty.

And whether it’s at the strategy or tactics level, data analytics are a game-changer for decision-making.

Process Automation

Automating routine tasks isn’t about replacing humans. It’s about freeing up human capacity for more strategic roles.

Not only does automation help businesses achieve efficiency, but it can also allow for scalability and new growth opportunities.

Digital Transformation Strategy vs Roadmap

Digital transformation roadmaps are often confused with digital transformation strategies. But here’s the difference:

A digital transformation strategy provides an overarching vision. Think of it as the “why” or “what” — that is, why a business needs to transform or what its goals are.

Namely, this would include an organization’s:

  • Objectives
  • Purpose
  • Desired outcomes

A digital transformation roadmap is the practical application of that strategy. Think of it as the “how” — specifically, how a company tackles its goals and strategies.

That includes:

  • Specific steps or tasks
  • Timelines
  • Milestones

Why a Roadmap Matters

Trying to wade into the vast digital landscape without a clear, carefully thought-out plan is a recipe for disaster. Here’s what makes roadmaps so critical.

They Make Your Strategy and Goals Achievable

Digital transformation is an ambitious endeavor, but it’s more manageable when it’s broken down into digestible, actionable steps.

A structured approach helps ensure that every piece of the digital puzzle aligns with the overarching strategy.

A strategy without a concrete roadmap leads to:

  • Wasted resources
  • Misaligned effort
  • Unmet objectives

Check out the following digital transformation examples for more info.

They Give Your Transformation Clarity and Structure

Technologies are ever-shifting, and so are business paradigms.

A roadmap offers a clear trajectory without ambiguity. Defining milestones, timelines, and deliverables provides teams with a sense of direction and purpose.

That creates alignment and collaboration, and everyone understands their role as a result.

Consider a retail store transforming into an e-commerce platform. Without a roadmap, that shift can quickly become overwhelming.

But with a roadmap, the team can follow a step-by-step process — website creation, digital marketing, etc. — with each person having clearly defined roles to keep the transformation on track.

They Mitigate Risks and Challenges

Digital transformation is rife with possible pitfalls. A roadmap can help identify and plan for these challenges in advance by setting tangible milestones and providing checkpoints to evaluate progress and change course if necessary.

Regular assessments based on the roadmap can prevent costly missteps and ensure that resources are used efficiently and that goals are met.

How to Create a Digital Transformation Roadmap: Step-by-Step

This section offers a definitive guide to constructing your transformation roadmap and enabling your organization to realize its digital aspirations.

Step 1: Assess Your Current State

First, take a deep look at where you are through the following two components:

Technological

  • Catalog your existing platforms and tools. Examine why they’re relevant to your operation and how efficient they are.
  • Identify gaps or inefficiencies in your current digital capabilities. For example, maybe you’re still relying on paper-based processes or failing to capture and utilize customer data.

Organizational

  • Explore your organization’s ethos. Is there resistance to change, or is the team excited about digital prospects?
  • Conduct a skills audit to see how adept with technology your staff is and determine their training needs.
  • Review existing digital processes. Some might be streamlined with automation, while others may need a complete overhaul.

Step 2: Define Strategic Goals

First, clearly outline what you aim to achieve. What vision do you have for the future? And what methods can you use to accomplish that vision?

Maybe your objectives are a better experience for customers, improved efficiency, or both.

Align these targets with the business’s larger objectives to ensure cohesion with broader goals, such as expanding to new markets.

Then, set measurable key performance indicators (KPIs) for each goal. For example, a 20% increase in sales could be a measurable goal.

Step 3: Engage Stakeholders and Senior Management

Digital transformation affects every facet of a business. So, stakeholder buy-in is crucial. Articulate to your team the long-term value and immediate benefits of this transformation.

You can address concerns and describe the rewards in:

  • Workshops
  • Presentations
  • One-on-one meetings

Establish a clear decision-making hierarchy. While input is vital, having a structure helps streamline decisions and aligns the team’s digital transformation efforts with the roadmap.

Step 4: Choose the Right Digital Technologies and Tools

There’s no shortage of technologies available. Select the tools that align best with your needs.

For example, you may incorporate:

  • AI tools
  • Cloud solutions
  • Advanced analytics
  • Tools that integrate with MS Teams
  • Hybrid work management software

But always consider the future. These tools shouldn’t just address current challenges — they should also be scalable for upcoming demands.

Lastly, be wary of sales pitches, flashy solutions, or too many tools. Stay grounded in your goals and a broader awareness of your company’s long-term path.

Step 5: Allocate Resources

Determine the budget for each component of your roadmap. That includes the cost of the following:

  • New technology purchases
  • Potential hires
  • Training programs

Time is another resource to consider. Set clear timelines, understanding that while some tasks might be accomplished quickly, others, like a shift in culture, might take longer.

Step 6: Develop a Management Strategy

A well-thought-out management strategy will help with your digital transformation roadmap’s implementation. Identify the key players who will lead this transformation. Define a clear governance structure regarding who will do what.

Establish regular check-ins. Whether they’re weekly, monthly, or quarterly, schedule reviews to address challenges and make course corrections.

Then, adopt project management tools to ensure intentional collaboration and communication. Here’s a good list of collaboration tools.

An effective management strategy should also include:

  • Channels for feedback
  • Training and upskilling
  • Contingency plans

Step 7: Conduct a Pilot Test

Instead of implementing the roadmap company-wide, it’s wise to start with a segment. Maybe there’s a department that’s most in need or most adaptable to change.

Operate this pilot test in a controlled environment so you can easily gauge its success and any potential issues.

After the test is complete, analyze its outcomes meticulously.

Ask yourself:

  • What worked?
  • What didn’t work?
  • Did issues stem from the new process or tool itself or the team’s ability to use it?

Step 8: Roll the Roadmap Out in Phases

After you analyze the pilot test’s results, set a plan for the additional phases. Depending on the size and nature of the business, this could be department-wise or solution-wise.

Be prepared that each phase will have unique challenges. The sales department may transition easily, but logistics might run into problems.

Encourage an iterative approach.

After each phase:

  • Gather insights
  • Make the necessary tweaks
  • Move to the next phase

Step 9: Solicit Feedback

Constructive feedback is the foundation of continuous improvement.

Employ tools like surveys or feedback forms and create the following feedback loop:

  • Collect feedback
  • Analyze the feedback
  • Make improvements
  • Gather feedback again

You’ll need both employee and customer perspectives. Employee feedback is useful for optimizing internal processes, whereas customer feedback gives you insights into customer experience and preferences.

4 Tips for Ensuring Your Digital Transformation Is Successful

Navigating a digital transformation can be challenging, but these tips will help you do it right:

Tip 1: Start With a Good Leadership Team

Business leaders stand at the helm of any digital transformation journey. Their ability to guide, inspire, and anticipate changes sets the tone for the entire organization.

As stated in a 2021 report by MIT Sloan Management Review, “Efforts to lead digital transformation are unlikely to be effective without a leader’s own affective digital transformation — one that makes purpose, engagement, and fairness as important to workplace success as data-driven agility and productivity.”

Tip 2: Engage Your Employees

Digital transformation isn’t just about technology. It’s also about people.

Making sure your employees understand and embrace the change is crucial. Workshops, training sessions, and initiating feedback can bolster their engagement.

Neglecting this aspect can lead to resistance and hinder progress.

Tip 3: Help Your Team Through Change Management

As businesses evolve digitally, changes are inevitable.

Proper change management practices, such as clear communication, adequate training, and constant support, can help ease these transitions.

For example, General Electric helped their team through a successful transformation in the 2010s by training and upskilling current employees and encouraging a culture of digital innovation.

Tip 4: Leverage Data to Improve Decision-Making

Data is as good as gold. Harnessing data-driven insights can inform and optimize the digital transformation process.

Companies like Netflix have masterfully used data analytics. They use it to tailor their content, optimize user experience, and drive innovation.

Every data point that can be collected from your operating activities and customer interactions needs to be compiled and stored.

How Digital Technology Can Transform Your Hybrid Workplace

Hybrid work and digital transformation are two trends in business that go hand in hand. Here’s how hybrid work can support your transformation:

By Reshaping Operations

Cloud-based project management and collaboration platforms break down geographical constraints. This encourages business strategy to become more decentralized and agile.

Post body:
A workplace management platform is an essential software solution for any organization that wants to enable hybrid work and transition to a flexible workforce. Workplace platforms help companies create safer, more flexible, and more delightful employees’ workplace experiences. Furthermore, it streamlines the day-to-day work-related processes that get in the way of great work. The key elements of a good, future-looking hybrid workplace platform are:

  • How easy it is for employees to manage their work-related schedules and book the spaces they need.
  • Is the system advanced enough, extensible, and highly customizable to support the agility of your organization?
  • Does the platform integrate with the 3rd party apps you need to execute your workplace strategy?

A workplace platform gives the office, facility, and HR managers a complete toolbox to enhance the workplace experience for the entire organization – remote, office, or hybrid employees. Let’s dig in for more details!

What is a Workplace Management Software?

Workplace software systems have almost always been with us. However, the world changed drastically over the last few years and so the workplace systems have to change too.

The previous generation of workplace systems was called Integrated Workplace Management Systems (IWMS). These complex, cumbersome software platforms were mostly used for managing the complexity of the real estate, as well as the space and facility management needs of corporate customers. In other words, the focus has always been on real estate and not really on the people. They’ve been resources management systems first and quite often only.

The focus of the workplace management software of the future though is more about managing the hybrid workforce, employee workplace experience, automation, extensibility, and ease of use. Technology is so deeply ingrained in our life and so the workplace must be too. However, in order to get there, workplace apps have to be at least as good as the apps we use on a daily basis, if not better.

Employee scheduling – Book from anywhere, work from anywhere

The shift to a hybrid work model means that employees no longer know for certain who will be in the office each day. Booking a day in the office when your team isn’t there may easily feel like a waste. You can help your employees coordinate and make it a lot easier to schedule visits and invite teammates to co-create and work together.

Your main focus when choosing a hybrid workspace management software should be the ease of use and potential reach of the application. The adoption of your scheduling platform, thus your employee satisfaction relies heavily on that. You really want to enable booking on all screens.

  • Web portal; We spend our working days in the browser and it is still the #1 utilized way of booking desks.
  • Mobile app; Your booking system must have an extremely easy-to-use and awesome mobile app for iOS and Android.
  • Integrated Calendars – Outlook or Google Calendar; Your system must be extremely well integrated with your organization’s calendar system.
  • Collaboration system – Teams or Slack; Your booking system must be where your people are – in your messaging app, like Microsoft Teams.
  • Extensibility – Google Chrome; Most people use Google Chrome and have your booking system deeply integrated into the browser can make it a million times easier to reserve a space.
  • More screens – Tablet apps; Some people prefer to directly book the space from the tablet mounted on the space.

We use many screens for many reasons in our daily life. Your booking software should be available anywhere in order to increase your employee adoption and satisfaction, thus your use of office space.

System Configuration, Extensibility, and Customization

The modern workplace management systems are highly customizable, configurable, and extensible to suit your need for agility. Some of the more important elements you should look for include:

  • Desk booking system; Empower employees to easily find and reserve shared or assigned desks directly on the floorplan. Desk booking software is essential to implement desk hoteling or hot desking strategy.
  • Meeting room booking system; Make it easy for your employees to find and book the right spaces for their meetings. Conference room scheduling systems are key to making hybrid work possible for your employees.
  • Workplace experience apps; Improve employees’ office experience with an easy-to-use mobile app and web portal. A good app and web portal will allow your employees to interact with the workplace and do the most important tasks such as book a desk, schedule a conference room, or see who’s coming to the office on Thursday.
  • Visitor management and reception app; Welcome guests with a delightful visitor management system that saves you time and keeps the workplace safe.
  • Health and safety management; Track the physical presence of employees and set appropriate limits on the number of people in the office.
  • Space and floorplans management; Easily manage your office assets, desks, rooms, parking spots, and any other resource available.
  • Integrations & 3rd party apps; Connect all the platforms you need to ensure a seamless hybrid work experience for your employees.
  • Extensibility and APIs; Have access to a well-documented and public API so that you can extend the platform the way you need.
  • Workplace analytics; Last but not least, you should collect, measure and analyze all data about your space utilization. This way you can adjust your space to the needs of your employees.

Why Do you Need a Hybrid Workplace Platform More Than Ever Before?

To compete in the most difficult job market and continue to grow your organization, you need to attract and retain top talent. With the rise of the flexible workforce and the receding pandemic, employees will rely even more on their workspace to connect and collaborate with their teammates. However, today’s workplaces can be very chaotic, inefficient, and disorganized and expose safety risks that could diminish the employee experience.

Workplace platforms empower you to enhance the workplace experience, and streamline internal operations, by bringing everything work-related into one solution. Furthermore, by using the desk reservation and conference room scheduling modules, you can build and rely on data to optimize your workspace utilization, and get more out of your real estate, thus reducing your costs.

It sounds simple, however, the benefits exceed many times the investment in an easy-to-use, customizable, and integrated workplace management system, such as OfficeRnD Workplace.

The desk booking component of a typical IWMS was usually handling only hot desk bookings via a kiosk installed in the office. This is a suboptimal user experience, for sure, and almost as bad as a hot desk booking template in excel.

The focus of the desk reservation systems of the future though is all about ease of use and employee workplace experience. Technology is so deeply ingrained in our life and so the workplace must be too. However, in order to get there, desk booking apps have to be at least as good as the apps we use on a daily basis, if not better.

Ease of use – Book from anywhere, work from anywhere

Your main focus when choosing a desk booking solution should be the ease of use and potential reach of the application. The adoption of your booking platform and your employee satisfaction relies heavily on that. You really want to enable booking on all screens.

  • Book from a Web portal; We spend our working days in the browser and it is still the #1 utilized way of booking desks.
  • Book from a Mobile app; Your desk booking system must have an extremely easy-to-use and awesome hot desk app for iOS and Android.
  • Integrate a Calendar solution – Outlook or Google Calendar; Your system must be extremely well integrated with your organization’s calendar system.
  • Book from a Collaboration system – Teams or Slack; Your booking system must be where your people are – in your messaging system, like Microsoft Teams so you have a seamless desk booking in Teams.
  • Book from Google Chrome; Most people use Google Chrome and having your booking system deeply integrated into the browser can make it like a million times easier to reserve a space. Providing your employees with an intuitive Google Workspace desk booking is a must.

We use many screens for many reasons in our daily life. Your desk scheduling software should be available anywhere in order to increase your employee adoption and satisfaction, thus your use of office space.

System Customization and Configuration

The modern desk scheduling systems are highly customizable and configurable to suit your need for agility. Some of the more important elements you should look for include:

  • Configurable interactive floorplan management, where everyone can see who’s in the office, as well as track available desks in real-time.
  • Delegated desk bookings; Such functionality enables your team leaders and managers to place bookings for their teams.
  • Recurring desk bookings; Arguably, one of the most important features that will make the lives of your employees a lot easier is recurring bookings. This way, they can build work patterns, like coming to the office every Tuesday and Thursday.
  • Private desk bookings; In some cases, you may want to book a desk or a space with limited visibility.
  • Desk booking policies; You may want to allow employees access to book desks in only certain areas, locations, zones, or neighborhoods.
  • Easy to use, or automated check-in system; You should also measure the true occupancy by requiring employees to check in or fully automating them through integrations.
  • Configurable and white-label web, mobile and integrations experience; Your employees should easily recognize your brand.
  • Collaboration and Smart Scheduling capabilities; Coming to the office is a team play, so you should enable your teams to collaboratively reserve spaces.
  • Advanced analytics; Last but not least, you should collect, measure and analyze all data about your desk utilization. This way you can adjust your space to the needs of your employees.

What are the Benefits of Desk Booking Software?

A good desk booking solution can help you create a more productive and collaborative workplace experience for your employees. Furthermore, by implementing desk hoteling or hot desking strategy, you can optimize your workspace utilization, and get more out of your real estate, thus reducing your costs.

Name: How To Improve Meeting Rooms Usage in Coworking Spaces
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Meeting rooms are a handy amenity that can help you attract prospects to your space or increase your alternative revenue stream while offering a valuable resource to people from within your community.
Post body:
Meeting rooms are a handy amenity that can help you attract prospects to your space or increase your alternative revenue stream while offering a valuable resource to people from within your community.

You’ve succeeded in the challenge of planning your meeting rooms and have already chosen the right ones for your coworking space.

Now the question is: Are you making the most out of your meeting rooms? How do you measure their usage? Can you increase bookings somehow?

Finding answers to these questions will give you valuable insights into how well your meeting rooms are performing, so you can use this information to evaluate and improve their usage.

There’s a number of key metrics you can monitor to measure meeting room usage including how often they’re booked, for how long, which meeting rooms are used the most, average bookings per day, week or month, peak or quiet hours, etc. Most of them can be easily tracked with coworking management software or various coworking apps.

The steps you can take to improve the areas which underperform depend on your business model – do members pay additionally for using meeting rooms or they are included in the plans you offer?

Improving usage of paid meeting rooms

Paid meeting rooms are usually popular in Serviced Offices (Executive Suites) and in some Coworking spaces. Two main factors lead to this:

  1. This happens in places where a lot of business meetings happen. Usually, members meet clients, partners, future investors and making the right impression is really important.
  2. Business meetings happen sporadically. Paying for a meeting room when the necessity comes fits your member’s needs (and wallets!) better than adding to their plans meeting rooms credits which, sometimes, they might not need.

Here’s what you can do to improve the usage of paid meeting rooms:

Attract external audiences

A successful approach to improve usage is to market your meeting rooms to the public. There are plenty of reasons why meeting rooms in coworking spaces are better than in hotels so there’s a natural interest towards them. 

One idea is to take advantage of marketplaces where you can list your meeting rooms. Of course, you would also like to optimize your website for search engines and fill it up with enough information and great photos to present your service properly.

Providing an option for online booking that shows live availability is another way you can attract more customers.

Read more about how to market meeting rooms: 6 Tips on How To Market Your Coworking Space Meeting Rooms.

Identify underutilized time slots and offer promotions

Time slots in the range of 2-5 pm are in most cases fully booked. It’s the time when most meetings happen – both internally and with external partners/clients.

Of course, every flex space is different, so you should find out what the trend is in your space. An analysis of usage will again require a dedicated solution, but it will be invaluable to have this data so you can know where to focus your efforts.

Once you identify the periods which are underutilized in your coworking space, you can think about offering discounts during those times.

Also, think about allowing bookings during non-business hours and setting lower price rates for them. After all, one of the coolest things about coworking is its flexibility, so giving your community members the opportunity the use your meeting rooms whenever they need, is an excellent thing to do.

Bundle free credits in recurring memberships

If your members have a membership plan, but they have to pay additionally for meeting rooms, there’s a real chance they’ll sometimes avoid it and go to the near cafe or use the open area in case they have an informal meetup.

However, if you bundle free credits for meeting rooms in their membership plan, they’ll be more willing to book and use a meeting room, as they won’t need to pay additionally for it.

At the end of the day, they do pay for it, but it’s the psychological aspect that’s important here.

Think about (discounted) prepaid credit bundles

Offer bundles of credits and give them at a lower price if people prepay for them.

It’s a win-win situation – your members receive a discount, you get a commitment for another 5 hours, for example.

Add discounts based on booking length

A great thing to do is to lower the price rate for longer bookings. An example structure would be to provide members with discounts for half-day bookings, full-day bookings, etc.

Of course, such flexibility will add some additional complexity to your everyday operations. You can eliminate such complexity with the help of coworking apps such as OfficeRnD which will help you manage meeting room bookings, billing, etc.

Improving the usage of free meeting rooms

Free meeting rooms for coworking members are widely popular in coworking spaces for various reasons.

It might be that your space is located in the suburbs of bigger and smaller cities and is not exposed to huge business traffic, so your members would usually have regular internal meetings (and making them paid will just be an inconvenience for them).

Or you might be focusing on memberships and increasing the amount of time a team or a member stays with you, and bundling in a free meeting room is a key differentiator.

But when members do not pay additionally for using a meeting room, there’s often a difference between what’s been booked and what’s been actually used.

How’s “booked” different from “used”?

Sometimes people book a meeting room but eventually don’t show up. Such ghost bookings can be very expensive for your coworking space. Another scenario you would like to avoid is rooms that aren’t used at their full capacity or are used for a shorter period than was actually booked.

Once you build a certain customer base, monitoring that on your own will be too much overhead, so you might think about turning to technology for help.

Make sure that the solution you pick has an easy to handle process both for you and your members – for example, allowing them to self-service themselves and control their bookings. Here are some ideas you could consider:

Member check-in to confirm a booking

This can be achieved with a tablet or a dashboard located at the entrance of a meeting room. If no one checks in 15 minutes, the coworking app will automatically remove the booking from the system, so other members can use the room.

Notifications and reminders

Use some kind of push notifications/reminder to the mobile app, which pings members before the meeting. Sometimes people forget to remove a booking when their meeting has been canceled. Sending them a push notification right before the booking with an easy way to cancel it is a possible approach.

Take advantage of IoT

Installing beacons in your meeting rooms which track movement, for example, is a good way to track what’s the actual usage of your meeting rooms (not only if people come, but how long they actually stay there).

Again the same logic can apply here if you connect such beacons with your booking management software – it can automatically delete a booking if no one shows up in 15 minutes.

Name: 6 Marketing Tips To Sell Coworking Meeting Rooms
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Marketing tactics like listing on marketplaces, improving your SEO, and making booking quick and easy can help you sell more of your coworking meeting rooms and bring in more revenue.
Post body:
Marketing tactics like listing on marketplaces, improving your SEO, and making booking quick and easy can help you sell more of your coworking meeting rooms and bring in more revenue.

Selling coworking meeting rooms means marketing bookable rooms to two audiences: your own members, and people outside your community who need a room for an hour, a day, or a recurring meeting. The tactics differ for each.

It’s worth doing this only after you’ve planned how many rooms and what types to have in your space. Once that’s set, it’s time to get creative.

Marketing your meeting rooms well takes work across a few areas: digital presence, presentation, on-site service, and promotion.

Below are 6 tips to help you attract more customers to your meeting rooms.

There’s an important distinction first: your approach should differ depending on whether you’re targeting people who are already part of your community or people outside it.

Marketing meeting rooms to your existing members takes less effort. You’ve already done the hard part: you brought these people into your space, and they’re using it.

Tracking and improving meeting room usage in your coworking space is a good way to encourage bookings and improve member satisfaction.

You can add meeting room credits to membership plans, or offer discounts on conference rooms to virtual members. Remove any friction from booking, accessing, and using the rooms.

Marketing to the public is harder and takes more effort. Here are our top 6 tips.

1/ Take advantage of marketplaces

Marketplaces like LiquidSpace, Coworker, and Croissant let you reach more people than you can through your own channels alone. These sites pull in steady traffic and can connect you with potential customers who’d never find your website on their own.

Coworking marketplaces aren’t only for hot desks. Operators can list private offices, meeting rooms, and event spaces too, and the quality of your listing directly affects your results.

They have filters like location, capacity, and amenities, so people get results that match their needs.

The presentation matters. Include enough information so people understand what you offer, and add strong photos so you stand out from everyone else on the list.

2/ Optimize your website for search engines and for people

Most people will first reach you through your website.

So how do you make sure it’s easy to find?

At its core, this means optimizing your site so it shows up when people search for specific keywords and phrases (for example, “meeting rooms”). A few tips follow.

Follow general SEO practices

Work on your page content, page speed, URLs, and meta descriptions. That’s the foundation. Here’s a solid rundown of the SEO essentials worth focusing on.

📍 Bonus tip: Local SEO is a smart focus, since searches for meeting rooms almost always include a location, like “meeting rooms in London.”

We’re not going deep on this here, but this is a good guide on what local SEO is and how to use it.

One newer angle: list your day passes, meeting rooms, and private offices as Products on your Google Business Profile, each with a price. Add an FAQ section to your site that answers the exact questions people (and AI answer engines like ChatGPT and Gemini) ask, such as “How much is a meeting room in [city]?” That helps you show up both in classic local search and in AI-generated answers.

Want to sharpen your SEO and pull in more bookings? Check out this expert-led video on SEO for coworking spaces.

Use content to boost your SEO

There are several reasons to invest time in a content strategy, like reaching your target groups and driving traffic to your website.

Blogs are one tool for that. Tips, how-tos, and any other information useful to the people you want to attract help both your search rankings and your overall brand reputation.

You can also create videos featuring your meeting rooms, booking process, and helpful tips to give potential customers a more engaging way to explore your services.

Make your website mobile-friendly

People spend a lot of time on their phones, so the odds someone visits your site from a smartphone are high. Google ranks mobile-friendly sites higher, and they give visitors a better experience.

Besides search engines, optimize for people

Put everything a potential customer needs to decide right on your website. If they can’t tell what you sell, they won’t buy.

Include location, rates, meeting facilities, room capacity, and even parking or public transport instructions. If you offer extra services or amenities, say so.

Be upfront about price. Buyers comparing venues move on fast if they have to call or email just to learn your hourly rate. For reference, CoworkingCafe’s Q1 2026 data put the national median meeting-room rate at $45 per hour in the US, though the spread runs from around $20 to $75 depending on the market.

3/ Make meeting rooms easy to book through your website

Your potential customers will probably follow this path:

Search in Google → land on your website → get enough information → book a meeting room

Cutting friction out of booking is how you turn interest into a reservation. Make booking easy, clear, and fast. And don’t forget to give your rooms memorable names.

Allow bookings at any time. Sometimes people need a room urgently, or it’s late in the evening, and they need one for the next morning.

The way to handle that is to show the live availability of your meeting rooms to the public and let people book directly.

You can do this with OfficeRnD Flex, which exposes your meeting rooms’ live availability on a public calendar so non-members can book a room online, on mobile, tablet, or desktop (screenshot below).

With OfficeRnD Flex you can also bundle free meeting room credits with membership plans, set booking policies and cancellation rules, add buffer time between bookings for cleanup, and offer add-on services like coffee or equipment directly inside the booking.

4/ Present your meeting rooms interactively

The old line “a picture is worth a thousand words” applies here.

Give a detailed visual presentation of your meeting rooms so people get a fuller sense of them while browsing.

Use great, high-quality photos. Hiring a professional photographer is worth it. They’ll know how to shoot the space from the right angle with the proper lighting.

The more interactive, the better. Consider 360° photos, video, or virtual tours. They cost more money and effort, but they show your rooms in the detail buyers want before they commit. A short vertical video walkthrough also works well on Instagram and TikTok, and answers the “what does it actually feel like?” question before anyone visits.

📍 Bonus tip: Including people in your photos and videos gives visitors a warmer, more human feel when they browse your gallery.

5/ Treat meeting rooms as a separate service

Provide excellent service

Cover everything from cleanliness to amenities to working multimedia and ventilation. You don’t want to ruin a business meeting over a lost HDMI cable or a broken AC during a heatwave.

Listen to people and respond to their needs

Maybe a need for soft drinks comes up at the last minute. Or they need an extra flipchart. Let people know they can reach out if they need something.

Even if it’s a service you don’t usually provide, it’s worth going the extra mile. Arranging their catering is probably much easier for you than for them, since you likely know good suppliers from events you’ve hosted. People appreciate that.

Take it personally

Welcome your external guests when they arrive, or pre-arrange access if they’re using your space after hours.

They don’t know your space, so make sure they know which areas they can use and how to find things like the kitchen or bathrooms.

It also helps to be clear about whether they have access to the community tea, coffee, and snacks.

📍 Bonus tip: Get to know the people coming to your meeting rooms. A quick chat about who they are and what they do is a good way to learn how you can help each other later.

6/ Public events, promotions, and pro bono

The more people come to your meeting rooms, the more likely they’ll think of you for their next meeting or event. Hosting public events helps a lot.

Think about what kind of event your target audience would want, then organize it.

Offering discounts to people or professional organizations, or a free room now and then, is another good way to promote your meeting rooms, and a genuine way to help out a local organization.

Name: How to Plan Your Coworking Space Meeting Rooms
Author: asen-stoyanchev
Short cards description: Getting the meeting room mix right comes down to 2 things: your location and your audience . Nail those, and you’ll make a far better call on what kind of rooms to build and how many of each.
Post body:
Getting the meeting room mix right comes down to 2 things: your location and your audience. Nail those, and you’ll make a far better call on what kind of rooms to build and how many of each.

Meeting rooms in a coworking space are the bookable rooms members and non-members use for calls, client meetings, team sessions, interviews, and events. They range from phone booths to formal conference rooms and event spaces.

They also make money. The most profitable operators generate 30 to 40% of revenue outside of workspace, and meeting rooms sit right alongside events and virtual mail in that mix. That makes them worth planning and managing carefully, aligned with what your space actually needs. Eventually, you’d also like to track and improve their usage so you can make the most out of them.

Demand is on your side here. Cushman & Wakefield reported that meeting room bookings surged worldwide in 2025: up 24.5% in APAC, 22% in the Americas, and 17.4% in EMEA. Rooms are becoming a revenue product, not just an amenity.

Here’s how location and audience shape the rooms you choose.

The role your location plays in planning meeting rooms

As with any other real estate business, location is of high importance as it defines what kind of potential customers you have access to.

And that applies not only for members that would rent a desk or an office long-term. But also for the people who come to your space ad-hoc (i.e. drop-ins).

We’ve identified two distinctive scenarios in terms of your coworking location – you are either near (or in the heart) of huge business traffic, or not.

How does a high amount of business traffic affect meeting room planning?

If you’re in the heart of a business district, your member base probably consists of companies that need a premium business location. The usual reason for paying a higher price to be there is to regularly meet with people outside of their business.

In other words, they have to make themselves accessible. Also, they want to make the right impression and they’ll need an appropriate meeting space to make this happen.

On the other hand, as a crosspoint of many meetings and work travels, your visitors may often be drop-ins. The chance they’ll need a quiet place to sit for a few hours or a meeting room to meet with a business associate is huge. It’s good to think about how to market your meeting rooms so you can attract these people.

To cover the needs of both your regular members and drop-ins, a higher number of meeting rooms might be required. And most likely the majority of meetings will be with clients of your members, which affects the proportion of “informal” and “formal” meeting places in your coworking space.

How does a lower amount of business traffic affect your meeting room planning?

If you’re not located near huge business traffic, it’s more likely the majority of your customers will stay long-term in your space and you’ll have fewer drop-ins.

Your members will still have meetings with clients, but it’s safe to assume that most meetings will be between teammates and coworkers.

You’ll still need formal meeting rooms. However, you’ll need to have enough informal meeting rooms, open leisure spaces, and joint areas, where teams can have a productive discussion and where community collaboration can happen.

The role your coworking audience plays in planning meeting rooms

If you’ve nailed down the first point from the 3 essentials of every successful coworking community, you probably have a good understanding of your target audience and have attracted like-minded professionals in your space.

The essence of their business and their personality define their daily workflow (calls, meetings, etc), or what kind of communication they have (formal, casual, etc).

Who’s in the building has shifted too. Corporate teams now make up roughly 27 to 28% of coworking users, and that share keeps growing. Team offices and meeting spaces are among the most in-demand products operators report, which changes the math on how many group rooms you plan for.

Let’s take a look at 2 examples that can influence how your meeting rooms should be planned:

Service-oriented companies and/or freelancers usually spend a huge amount of time on calls or meeting clients and partners. It’s safe to say that you’ll need a lot of phone booths in place to accommodate the higher number of calls. Also, meeting rooms would probably have to be equipped with coffee and water for eventual client meetings.

Product-oriented teams are mostly focused on building a product, not selling it. Those guys would usually have regular internal team meetings and will need private hang-out places to catch up with colleagues over a cup of coffee. They will also need a whiteboard/multimedia to write notes and present ideas visually.

The type of your audience and its daily work routine are important factors to be considered. They will give you the direction in which you need to focus on when choosing the meeting rooms in your coworking space.

Choosing the right type of meeting rooms

In the term “meeting rooms” we include everything from hangout places where your members can meet, chill and chat, to phone booths, to big conference rooms. Based on the meeting intention, we’ve divided meeting rooms into the following types:

Informal meeting rooms and spaces

These are hangout places, phone booths, and smaller meeting rooms that host just a few people and are generally not meant for long discussions. They usually don’t have much natural light, are not that spacious but still provide the essentials for a short meeting or a call.

You have to book some of them, others are ruled by first come, first served. People usually use them for informal or semi-formal meetings or calls.

It’s where your coworkers can chat with each other, or host job interviews. The small meeting rooms are normally equipped with a whiteboard and basic multimedia (TV), so you can make presentations and draft quick ideas with the team.

This type of “meeting rooms” don’t need to be located near the entrance, but should be easily accessible for your coworking members (from all floors, offices and open areas).

To decide how much space to dedicate to such places, or how to combine them, think about your members’ needs first. A few questions that can help you with that:

  • Do your members make a lot of calls on a daily basis? If they do, you’ll need more small rooms and phone-booths.
  • Do your members need discussions to happen in private? If yes, well closed-up meeting rooms will be better.
  • Do coworkers make plenty of informal discussions? If yes, focus on leisure and hangout places.

Formal meeting rooms

These meeting rooms are usually more spacious, have more natural light, and are more representative. They are used for formal meetings with potential clients and business partners.

Meeting rooms from that type should be equipped with whiteboards and multimedia, as presentations often happen there. Additional services like coffee and water should also be an option.

Another thing to have in mind – this type of meeting room should be easily accessible, so it’s best to locate them near the entrance of the building, preferably on the ground or first floor.

Boardrooms

These are high-luxury meeting rooms with a lot of amenities and services included directly in the price. They are suitable for formal meeting with partners, clients, investors.

The price is high, but these are the rooms where you would like to meet a high profile client or your potential investor. They are classy and are more typical for business centers, rather than coworking spaces.

Adding a boardroom might make sense if your coworking space is located in a global business city or district, where a lot of entrepreneurs, investors, and high-profile business people meet.

Event spaces and Training rooms

These rooms often host public events, which attract not only your members but people outside of your space as well. They are a good “tool” you can use to welcome external audiences and promote your space.

It’s best if they are designed in a flexible way – you should be able to move furniture easily and have some kind of free space where you can serve catering or that can be utilized for anything else related to the event.

A word of caution – event spaces and training rooms are not your typical meeting space. They take a lot of space and a lot of effort goes into utilizing them, so choosing to create one should be aligned with your strategy.

How much of your space should meeting rooms take?

There’s no universal split that works for every space, and desk density alone does little for profitability. Product mix and layout matter more, so plan rooms against real member demand rather than a formula.

A common starting point operators use is roughly 60% for workstations (open desks and private offices), 30% for collaboration and amenities (meeting rooms, lounges, kitchen, breakout areas), and 10% for operations (reception, storage, IT). Treat it as a baseline to adjust from, not a rule. Then let member feedback and booking data tell you where to add or cut rooms.

One practical rule for sizing: match the layout to the work, not just the headcount. A 6 to 7-person meeting room usually needs around 150 to 160 square feet, while a large room for 14 to 16 people runs closer to 450. Leave room to rearrange furniture for workshops and training.

Turning meeting rooms into a revenue product

Rising demand only pays off if you price and manage rooms well. The OfficeRnD FlexIndex Q4 2025 report, built on data from 3,500+ flex locations, found the price per hour of booking jumped from $40.71 in Q3 to $44.38 in Q4 2025, and it flagged hourly pricing as one of the most actionable levers operators can pull. If your rooms are consistently busy but your hourly yield is flat, you’re giving away free upgrades.

A few policy decisions, enforced consistently, do most of the work:

  • Peak and off-peak pricing tiers
  • Minimum booking durations for prime slots
  • Standardized buffers and cancellation windows
  • No standing exceptions for the same person every week

OfficeRnD Flex is the coworking management platform that lets you set hourly and daily room rates, cancellation policies, check-in requirements, and business-hours rules, so pricing runs the same way every day. For non-members, its Growth Hub embeds booking straight into your website, so drop-ins can find and pay for a room without filling out a contact form.

But it will add some extra value to your services. (For more apps and tools for your community you can check How to Improve Engagement With Coworking Apps and How to Engage Your Coworking Community Online with Video Rooms.)

We got inspired to tell you more about Freckle because CoWork Me, a client of ours, saw amazingly good results after implementing the dashboard app.

So we sat down to interview Tim Sullivan, Business Specialist at Freckle Dashboards, with the hope that more coworking spaces will benefit from this cool piece of technology that can make the idea of a real-time members dashboard a reality.

Here it is, read below!

How would you describe the value of the ‘Freckle Dashboards’ for both coworking members and coworking space operators?

The Freckle Dashboard strengthens member connections within coworking spaces.

As a Coworking space operator, not only do you want your space occupied at full capacity but you want everyone to feel part of something bigger. By putting important community info on display, members can engage with activities, events, and club news whilst also have a direct connection to the vibe of your space. With the easy visual display of Freckle dashboards, members can have their finger on the pulse of your community and be in sync with what other members in the building are all about, who does what and how you can contact them. The dashboard is fully customizable, so you can choose what your members should be informed about. There are many opportunities to add a bit of fun to it, including live updates of the Spotify track which is being played at that moment in the space or the option to ask engaging questions such as ‘Star Wars or Star Trek?’ and watch the live replies on the screen.

As a member, you can get a quick glance overview of the coworking space that gives you enough information to feel empowered within your community. You can also have your 5-minutes of fame on the screen showcasing and promoting your brand, which can be a great conversation starter if you’re the new kid on the block.

Whether it is a motivational quote, upcoming seminar or images of member’s dogs on a slideshow, it is a sure way to keep everyone engaged.
